mainEntity.name: What should I do if my veneer falls off?

acceptedAnswer.text: If your veneer has come off, keep the veneer safe (ideally in a small container or sealed bag) and contact your dental practice as soon as possible to arrange an assessment. Avoid eating on that side of your mouth if the underlying tooth feels sensitive or sharp. Do not attempt to reattach the veneer using household glue or adhesive, as these products are not designed for oral use and could cause additional damage to the tooth or veneer. Depending on the condition of the veneer and the tooth beneath, your dentist will advise whether rebonding or replacement is appropriate.

mainEntity.name: Is it painful when a veneer comes off?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the individual and the underlying tooth. Some patients experience no discomfort at all when a veneer detaches, particularly if the bond has been gradually weakening. Others may notice sensitivity to temperature, air, or pressure on the exposed tooth surface. If you do experience pain or significant sensitivity, this is a good reason to seek professional assessment promptly. Exposed dentine — the layer beneath enamel — can be sensitive, so your dentist may apply a protective measure whilst the tooth awaits definitive treatment.

mainEntity.name: Can a veneer that has come off be put back on?

acceptedAnswer.text: In some cases, yes — but this depends entirely on the clinical condition of both the veneer and the tooth, which must be assessed by a dentist. If the veneer is undamaged and the tooth beneath is healthy and free from decay, rebonding may be possible. However, if the tooth has developed decay, the veneer is chipped or damaged, or the original preparation is no longer suitable for bonding, a new veneer may be required. Your dentist is best placed to advise you following a proper examination.

mainEntity.name: How can I tell if my veneer is starting to fail before it comes off?

acceptedAnswer.text: Early signs that a veneer may be failing include increased sensitivity in the tooth, a change in the way your bite feels, a visible or palpable gap at the edge of the veneer, rough or sharp edges that were not there before, or discolouration at the margins. Regular dental check-ups are valuable precisely because dentists can often identify early signs of veneer wear or marginal failure before the patient notices them. If you notice any of these signs between appointments, it is worth contacting your practice to arrange an earlier review.

mainEntity.name: Does teeth grinding cause veneers to come off?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, bruxism (teeth grinding) is a known risk factor for veneer failure. The repetitive, high-force movements associated with grinding — particularly during sleep — can place significant stress on the adhesive bond and on the veneer material itself. Over time, this can cause veneers to crack, chip, or detach. Patients who grind their teeth are often advised to wear a custom-made night guard to protect their dental restorations. If you suspect you may be grinding your teeth, discussing this with your dentist before or after veneer treatment is important.

mainEntity.name: Are some types of veneers more likely to come off than others?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both porcelain and composite veneers can come off, though their failure modes differ somewhat. Composite veneers, being softer, may wear down or chip more readily, whilst porcelain veneers are harder but can fracture under significant impact or grinding. Neither material is immune to detachment. The quality of the bonding process, the preparation of the tooth, the patient's oral habits, and the clinical expertise involved in placement all have a substantial influence on how well any veneer remains in place over time.
